title: Tamsin and the Hymn
premise: Mirabel Sterling, a pest controller who copes with the world by documenting it, is hired to deal with an infestation in the village of Hollowmere—only to find handprints on the church rafters that belong to no living villager. The bell that rang at midnight was melted down in 1911, and the hymn the congregation hums in their sleep was written by a vicar who drowned eleven children to keep his parish alive through famine. As Mirabel digs into the parish records she realizes the village renews its bargain every hundred years, and this time they have chosen her as the offering. In the end she must choose between burning the truth and escaping alone, or staying until sunrise to sing the hymn back at the thing in the tower—buying Hollowmere another century at the cost of her own name being erased from every record she ever wrote.
about_author: B. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in rural England, where the paperwork was often stranger than the parishioners. They write horror about people who believe that if you can name a thing precisely enough, it cannot hurt you.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She takes a routine pest call in Hollowmere, noting in her logbook the odd phrasing of the request: 'something with fingerprints.' The village feels watchful, doors closing as she passes. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking a lifetime of wanting to be needed but never noticed.

chapters.title: Grease and Ash
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In the church vestry she finds smudged prints on the rafters—human, but pressed into soot that hasn't existed since the coal fire of 1911. Her documentation ritual steadies her. Emotional beat: the comfort of evidence, and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At midnight the church bell rings; the plaque below the tower says it was melted for scrap in 1911. She photographs it; the photos show only an empty belfry. Emotional beat: the vertigo of a fact refusing to hold still.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The oldest villager insists the bell never melted—'we lent it, dear, and it comes back to be rung.' Everyone else denies hearing anything. Emotional beat: Mirabel realizes the village isn't lying to her; they're lying to themselves, together, on purpose.

chapters.title: Parish Paperwork
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. In the county archive she finds the 1911 register: a vicar named Edmund Halloway, eleven children's names struck through, and a hymn in his handwriting titled 'The Keeping.' Emotional beat: the thrill of research curdling into dread as the pattern emerges.

chapters.title: The Hymn
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She hums the hymn's melody from the manuscript and that night hears the whole village humming it in their sleep, windows glowing. Emotional beat: complicity—she has carried something into herself that cannot be put back.

chapters.title: What the Prints Belong To
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The prints on the rafters are small, child-sized, and arranged like a ladder climbing toward the belfry. She documents them and the ink of her own logbook pages begins to fade. Emotional beat: the horror that her records—her prayers—are being unwritten.

chapters.title: Invited
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The vicar's 1911 diary, hidden in the vestry floor, reveals the bargain: feed the tower a name each century and the parish survives famine, war, plague. The village council signed a new invitation last month—with a blank for the name. Emotional beat: cold clarity; she was never hired, she was chosen.

chapters.title: The Council of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: the council chairman, Mr. Petch, who signed the invitation. He is not a monster; he is a father whose daughter was sick all winter, and the bargain worked. Emotional beat: the seductive arithmetic of sacrifice—his guilt braided with relief.

chapters.title: Doors That Close Politely
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Every exit from the village is 'closed for repairs'; her car's tyres are flat, her phone shows no signal but full bars. The villagers are kind, gentle, apologetic. Emotional beat: the horror of being unmade by politeness.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Name
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Cross-referencing the struck-through names, she finds ten children drowned in 1911—but the eleventh name is smudged, as if the ink itself is afraid. The tower wants what it was owed and has waited a century to collect. Emotional beat: obsession as self-protection.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous's POV. She was the eleventh child's sister; her family gave the name to the tower and she has kept the secret for ninety years, humming the hymn every night to keep it asleep. Emotional beat: the corrosive cost of loyalty to a lie.

chapters.title: The Smudge
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The smudged name is Mrs. Aldous's sister, Edith—but Edith didn't drown; she climbed. The prints on the rafters are hers, still climbing, still waiting to be rung home. Emotional beat: grief for a girl the village spent a century forgetting on purpose.

chapters.title: Nightfall, Night One
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She barricades herself in the vestry as the bell begins to ring and the village sleepwalks toward the churchyard, faces upturned, humming. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into resolve—she will not be a name in someone else's ledger.

chapters.title: The Long Dark
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Through the night the thing in the belfry tests her: Edith's voice through the door, then her own mother's, then her own, reading her fading logbook aloud. Emotional beat: the temptation to surrender to being remembered by something, even this.

chapters.title: What Petch Knows
chapters.summary: Mr. Petch's POV. He comes at dawn to apologize and confess: the council has done this before; his own grandfather signed the 1911 page. He offers to let her go if she leaves before the next midnight. Emotional beat: cowardice dressed as mercy, and Mirabel seeing through it.

chapters.title: Burning the Records
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She could burn the parish register and the invitation, ending the bargain and dooming the village—or herself. Her documentation instinct wars with her survival instinct. Emotional beat: the realization that truth kept safe in a drawer has never saved anyone.

chapters.title: The Second Midnight
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She chooses neither escape nor burning: she walks into the churchyard as the village converges and begins to sing 'The Keeping' aloud, the true verses Halloway cut from the hymn—the ones naming what was invited in. Emotional beat: courage as an act of record-keeping.

chapters.title: The Bell Speaks
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The tower answers; the melted bell becomes visible, ringing itself, and Edith's prints begin to glow on the rafters like a ladder burning downward. The village wakes mid-hum. Emotional beat: awe—the moment the lie becomes too heavy to carry and shatters.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She negotiates with what waits in the belfry: not a name, but the truth, spoken by every villager at once—the debt acknowledged, Edith's name restored. The bell falls silent. The price: the thing will return in a hundred years, and someone must remember how to answer. Emotional beat: exhausted, hard-won truce.

chapters.title: The Unwritten
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She leaves Hollowmere alive but finds her name gone from her own logbooks, her licences, her mother's memory of her middle name—the tower took its toll in record. Only the villagers remember her, and they keep her file like a relic. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in identity, and choosing to bear it.

chapters.title: A Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, epilogue. One hundred years is a long time, but documents outlast their writers: she leaves the true hymn, the full register, and instructions in a new archive, addressed to whoever is called next. The last line of her final logbook: 'If you are reading this, you were invited. Sing anyway.' Emotional beat: hope as an inheritance, loyalty finally aligned with truth.
